title.plain: Money you can check |yourself|, on an ordinary computer, forever.
title.curious: A full node that costs |the same in thirty years| as it does today.
title.technical: Constant validation cost |by construction|, not by policy.

plain: Every cryptocurrency has a problem it does not talk about much: the more people use it, the more expensive it becomes to check it yourself. Checking is what keeps it honest. So the more successful it gets, the fewer people can hold it to account, and the more everyone has to take someone else at their word.
Cairn is built so that never happens. Whatever the chain does, however many people use it, checking it costs the same. Not less than today, not more. The same.
curious: On existing chains, running a full node means holding the entire set of unspent outputs, and that set grows with adoption. Bitcoin sits at gigabytes, Ethereum needs a machine most people do not own. The cost of verification rises with usage, so success quietly pushes verification into data centres.

Cairn puts a hard ceiling on that cost. A node keeps a bounded working set in full and everything else as sixty four hashes. Not a compromise on validation: a node still checks every rule on every block. It just never has to hold more than it holds today.
technical: Validation state is split in two. A bounded hot set of 131072 notes is held in full, in a sparse Merkle tree. Everything older lives in an append-only Merkle forest, which a node carries as sixty four roots and nothing else.

Adding a leaf to that forest needs only the roots, which is what makes a pruned node possible: it can extend the accumulator without holding it. Spending a fallen note takes an inclusion proof supplied by the spender, checked against roots the node already has.

title.plain: What a computer on this network actually holds
title.curious: What a full node actually holds

plain: Think of it as a drawer and a cave. Every computer on the network keeps the drawer in full: the money that has moved recently, {capacity} notes at most, which comes to about {megabytes}. That is the whole cost, and it never grows.
Everything older goes down to the cave. Nobody keeps the cave. What every computer keeps instead is sixty four short fingerprints, enough to check that anything pulled back up really was down there.
curious: The hot set is bounded at {capacity} notes, roughly {megabytes} held in full by every node. When it is full, the oldest notes fall to the cold set.

The cold set is unbounded and nobody stores it. Every node keeps sixty four hashes that stand for all of it. Spending something from down there means bringing a proof, which your own wallet has been keeping for you.
technical: Hot set: {capacity} notes maximum, held in a sparse Merkle tree, about {megabytes} at capacity. Eviction is by age, oldest first, in batches at block boundaries.

Cold set: an append-only Merkle forest, sixty four roots. A spend from it carries an inclusion proof; proofs may lag up to 32 blocks, and a note that has just fallen stays spendable without one for 64 blocks.

plain: This site is not just a node. It is a node plus a very large card index: for every note that has ever existed it remembers who was paid, when, and what became of it, so that you can type an address into the box above and be told what it holds. The chain itself refuses to make anybody carry that. It is here so that it is not there.

It costs about {perNote} bytes for every note that has ever existed, and it never stops growing. Keeping the cave, which this computer also does, costs about {coldPerNote} bytes for each note that has fallen. An ordinary node keeps neither and pays for neither.
curious: The index is the explorer's own growing cost, and it is the larger of its two by about seven times: {perNote} bytes for every note ever created, against {coldPerNote} bytes for every note that has fallen into the cold set. Both are unbounded, and both are carried by whoever chooses to offer this service.
A plain node carries neither. Its memory does not move with the cold set at all, which is the claim the whole design rests on, and this page is what an exception to it looks like.
technical: Owner to notes, note to record, transaction identifier to location, and one movement recorded per credit and per debit. Nothing is ever removed, so the size is a function of the chain's whole history rather than of its current state.

Measured on the running implementation: {perNote} bytes per note ever created for the index, {coldPerNote} bytes per fallen note for an archiving node's cold set, and no slope at all for a node that keeps only the sixty four roots.

None of it is bounded by a rule. One block filled to the byte limit can be three thousand dust notes to three thousand fresh addresses, which is about 1.6 MB of index for that one block, and about 810 GB a year at a block a minute. Whoever mines that block pays nothing for it: the fee floor is a node's own policy about what it will carry, not a rule of the chain.

plain: These are the rules every computer on the network agrees on. They are not settings anyone can change on their own machine: two computers that disagreed on any single line here would end up building two different chains while each believed it was on the same one.
They are read directly from a running node, so this page cannot be out of date.
curious: Every value below is consensus. None of them is an operator flag. A node picks them by naming a network, never one at a time, because a node running one different value silently follows a different chain.
Read live from the node serving this page.
technical: The full consensus parameter set, read live from ConsensusParams on the node behind this page. Every field is committed to by the rules that use it; none is configurable per node.

blocks.plain: A block is a page in the ledger. Roughly once a minute, someone finds a valid one, and everything in it becomes settled. Each page points back at the one before it, which is why nobody can quietly rewrite an old one.
blocks.curious: Blocks arrive about once a minute. The chain is chosen by accumulated work rather than by length, so the branch that took the most computing to build is the one every node follows.
blocks.technical: Fork choice is by cumulative work. Ties keep the branch already followed, and a switch is applied atomically. Difficulty retargets over a 90 block LWMA window with clamped solve times and a factor of four per retarget cap.

block.plain: Everything below was fixed the moment this block was found. The long strings are fingerprints: change one letter anywhere in the block and every one of them changes completely.
block.curious: The header commits to the transactions in the block and to the whole note set as it stands afterwards. The nonce is what the miner varied until the block identifier came out below the target.
block.technical: The identifier is a domain-separated BLAKE3 hash of the canonical header encoding, and it is what proof of work is measured against. Timestamps are checked against the median of the previous eleven blocks, not against the parent.

coinbase.plain: This is where new money comes from. Whoever found this block is paid for the work, and that payment is the only way CAIRN is ever created. Nobody was given any at the start.
coinbase.curious: The coinbase pays the block reward plus every fee in the block. The reward halves on a fixed schedule and then stops falling at a floor that is paid forever.
coinbase.technical: Coinbase outputs take identifiers derived from the transaction, which commits to the height, so two blocks paying identical outputs at different heights cannot collide. The extra field is capped at 64 bytes and gives a miner search space beyond the header nonce.

transfers.plain: Each of these is somebody sending money to somebody else. Money here is not a balance that goes up and down: it is a set of notes, and sending means tearing up notes you hold and writing new ones.
transfers.curious: Transfers consume notes and create new ones, in the style of unspent outputs. What a transfer does not consume, it pays as a fee to whoever mined the block.
transfers.technical: Transfer identifiers exclude signatures and witnesses. That kills malleability, and it is also what lets a stale inclusion proof be swapped for a fresh one without invalidating anything downstream.

transaction.plain: A transaction tears up some notes and writes new ones. The total written can never exceed the total torn up. Whatever is left over goes to whoever found the block, as a fee.
transaction.curious: Inputs name the notes being spent, outputs are the notes being created. A signature per input proves the spender owned it.
transaction.technical: Each signature commits to the network, the version, the transaction identifier, the input index, and the value and owner of the note being spent. Committing to the spent note is the lesson from the transactions that could be tricked about their own value.

inputs.plain: These are the notes being torn up. Each one was written by an earlier transaction, and each can only be torn up once.
inputs.curious: Each input names a note and proves the right to spend it. Held where tells you whether every node still had that note, or whether the spender had to bring a proof.
inputs.technical: A hot witness needs nothing: the node holds the note. A cold witness carries the note, its position in the forest, and an inclusion proof verified against roots the node already has.

outputs.plain: These are the new notes. Each belongs to one address and can be spent exactly once, later, by whoever holds the matching secret.
outputs.curious: Each output is a value locked to a public key. Its identifier comes from the transaction that made it plus its position in the list.
outputs.technical: Note identifiers are the source transaction identifier and an index. Ordering over identifiers is defined so the note set has one canonical enumeration, which the state commitment depends on.

address.plain: An address is a public name you can hand out safely. Anyone can see what it holds. Only the person with the matching secret can spend it, and that secret never appears here or anywhere on this site.
address.curious: This page is built from an index over the whole chain, which is a service the explorer provides and the protocol deliberately does not: no node keeps a map from owners to notes.
address.technical: Ed25519 keys, with two restrictions beyond the standard: small order keys are rejected at construction, and non-canonical encodings are refused so two byte strings can never name one key.

holdings.plain: The individual notes this address is holding. A balance is just what they add up to.
holdings.curious: State tells you which notes every node still holds and which have fallen. A wallet keeps proofs for the fallen ones, so it can still spend them.
holdings.technical: Fallen notes need a proof at spend time. A wallet tracks the position and refreshes the proof as the forest grows; the node accepts a proof up to 32 blocks stale.

note.plain: One note. It was written once, it belongs to one address, and it can be torn up once. That is the whole life of it.
note.curious: A note is an unspent output: a value and an owner. It is never modified, only created and consumed.
note.technical: The leaf committed to the accumulator is a domain-separated hash over the identifier, the value and the owner, so a note cannot be moved between positions or reinterpreted.

pool.plain: Transfers that have been announced but are not settled yet. They are waiting for someone to find a block to put them in.
pool.curious: The mempool as this node sees it. Every node keeps its own, so what you see here is one node's view, not a network-wide truth.
pool.technical: Selection is deterministic in identifier order, so the order a miner walks the pool does not depend on arrival order. A transfer conflicting with a pooled one is refused rather than replacing it: choosing between conflicting spends is a fee policy, and there is no fee market yet to decide it.

holders.plain: Who holds the most. On a test network this says very little: it is mostly whoever left a computer mining the longest.
holders.curious: Computed from the explorer index, counting unspent notes per owner. An owner can hold any number of addresses, so this is a view of addresses, not of people.
holders.technical: Balances are the sum of unspent notes per public key over the followed branch. Reorganisations rebuild the index rather than unwinding it.

emission.plain: New money appears only as payment for the work of finding blocks. The amount halves every so often, then stops falling and stays at a small figure forever, so there is always a reason to keep the network running.
emission.curious: Halving every 1051200 blocks, from 50 CAIRN down to a permanent floor of 0.01 CAIRN per block. Around 105 million CAIRN exist before the floor takes over. How long a halving period lasts depends on the block time, which is listed above for this network.
emission.technical: A chain that promises verifiability in thirty years cannot rest its security budget on the open question of whether fee revenue alone is sufficient. The tail is a deliberate answer to that, at a known and small rate of dilution.

cost.plain: This is the whole point of Cairn. The drawer has a ceiling, so the cost of taking part has a ceiling. The cave can grow without limit and it still costs every computer exactly sixty four fingerprints.
cost.curious: Note the shape of it: the bounded part is bounded by rule, not by convention, and the unbounded part is carried as a constant. That is what makes the cost of a full node flat over time.
cost.technical: The forest is append-only, and adding a leaf needs only the roots. That is the property the whole design turns on: a node that holds none of the set can still extend the accumulator correctly.

learn.title: What Cairn is, and why it is built this way

plain: Eight short pieces. No prior knowledge assumed. If a word appears that you do not know, it is explained before it is used.
curious: Eight pieces, assuming you know roughly what a blockchain, a wallet and a miner are.
technical: Eight pieces, at the level of the design document. Numbers and structures rather than analogies.

title.curious: Success pushes verification into data centres

plain: A cryptocurrency works because lots of separate people check it. Nobody is in charge, so the checking is what stops anyone cheating.

But on existing systems, checking gets more expensive the more the system is used. At some point an ordinary person cannot do it any more, and has to trust a company that can. The system then depends on trusting a handful of companies, which is exactly what it was built to avoid.
So the more successful it gets, the more it drifts back into the thing it was meant to replace.
curious: A full node holds the set of unspent outputs and validates every rule against it. That set grows with adoption, so the cost of independent verification rises with usage.

The usual response is that hardware gets cheaper. Perhaps, but the direction is still wrong: the number of independent verifiers falls as the system succeeds. Light clients do not fix it, they change who you trust.
Cairn treats this as the design problem, not as an operational detail.
technical: UTXO set growth is unbounded in every deployed design. State expiry, statelessness and various accumulator schemes all address it; most either move the cost elsewhere or need a trusted setup.

The thesis here: put a hard ceiling on the state a validator must hold, and make the unbounded remainder carriable in constant space, without a trusted setup and without weakening what a node actually verifies.

title.plain: Money as notes, not as a balance
title.curious: Notes, which is to say unspent outputs

plain: Cairn does not keep an account with a balance that goes up and down. It keeps notes, the way cash keeps banknotes.

A note has a value and an owner. It is written once, and it can be torn up once. To send someone 30 when you hold a note worth 50, you tear up the 50 and write two new notes: one for 30 to them, one for 20 back to yourself.
This sounds like a detail. It is not: because a note is never modified, only created and destroyed, a computer can forget an old note entirely and still be certain about the ones that are left.
curious: The unspent output model, as in Bitcoin, rather than accounts. A note is a value locked to a public key, identified by the transaction that made it and its index in the outputs.

Immutability is the reason this model was chosen here. An account balance has to be read and written, so the account must be held. A note is created once and consumed once, which lets a node hold a commitment rather than the note itself.
technical: Note identifiers are (source transaction, output index). Ordering is defined over identifiers so the note set has one canonical enumeration, which the state commitment depends on.

Transfer identifiers exclude signatures and witnesses. This gives malleability resistance, and more importantly it means a stale inclusion proof can be replaced by a fresh one without changing any identifier that anything else committed to.

title.technical: The hot set: a bounded sparse Merkle tree

plain: Every computer on the network keeps one drawer. In it are the notes that have moved recently, and there is a hard limit on how many fit: 131072.

That limit is not a suggestion or an average. It is a rule the whole network agrees on, so the drawer can never grow past it, no matter how popular Cairn becomes. Full, it comes to about 107 megabytes. That is a fraction of a phone.
When the drawer is full and new notes need room, the oldest ones are taken out and moved to the cave.
curious: A bounded set of 131072 notes, held in full by every node, in a sparse Merkle tree so the state commitment can be recomputed cheaply. About 107 MB at capacity, measured on the running implementation.
Eviction is by age, oldest first, in batches at block boundaries. Every node evicts the same notes at the same height, because the rule is consensus.
technical: 131072 notes, sparse Merkle tree, persistent through structural sharing so a reorganisation can restore the previous root without a rebuild. 813 bytes per note measured, giving about 107 MB at capacity.
The tree is the one part of the design with clear room left: a leaner representation is the most valuable remaining optimisation, and it changes no rule.

title.curious: The cold set, which nobody stores
title.technical: The cold set: an append-only Merkle forest

plain: Everything that falls out of the drawer goes to the cave. The cave has no size limit, and here is the surprising part: nobody keeps it. Not one computer on the network stores what is down there.

What every computer keeps instead is sixty four short fingerprints. They are enough to answer one question: if someone claims a particular note is down in the cave, is that true? Yes or no, with certainty, without ever having seen the cave.
Sixty four fingerprints, whether the cave holds a thousand notes or a thousand billion.
curious: An append-only Merkle forest: a list of perfect binary trees, held as their roots. A node keeps sixty four hashes and nothing else, regardless of how many notes have fallen.

The critical property is that adding a leaf needs only the roots. That is what makes a pruned node possible. It can extend the accumulator correctly while holding none of it, which is not true of a plain Merkle tree.
technical: Sixty four roots, one per possible tree height. On insertion the new leaf rides on the right of every merge, so the trees it swallows are its own siblings in order: the inclusion proof falls out of the addition itself, at no extra cost.
Removal is batched and verified against the pre-block root before anything is applied, then pending proofs are refreshed, so two cold spends in the same block cannot invalidate each other.

plain: If nobody keeps the cave, how do you spend a note that has fallen into it? You bring the proof yourself.

Your wallet has been quietly keeping it for you since the day the note fell, and keeping it current. You do not do anything: it is just there when you spend. The network checks it against those sixty four fingerprints and either accepts it or does not.
So the cost of remembering an old note sits with the one person who cares about it, instead of with every computer on the network forever. That single move is what makes the whole thing work.
curious: The spender supplies an inclusion proof, verified against roots the node already holds. Your wallet tracks the position of each of your fallen notes and refreshes the proof as the forest grows.

Two windows make this survivable in practice. A proof may be up to 32 blocks stale, so a wallet that fell slightly behind is not refused. And a note that has only just fallen stays spendable with no proof at all for 64 blocks, because every node still has it.
technical: A proof is checked against the cold set as it stands, and against nothing else. Earlier versions accepted one matching any of the last thirty two states, so a transfer written while a block was being found was not invalid through no fault of its author. That was half a rule: removing a note folds along the path the proof carries, an old path does not reach the root that is there now, so the removal did nothing and the note stayed to be spent again. A transfer's identifier excludes its witness, so one that waited too long is the same transfer offered again with a fresh proof.
GRACE_BLOCKS is 64 and GRACE_NOTES is 8192. Archivists, which are optional nodes that do keep the cold set, can rebuild a proof for someone who lost theirs.

title.plain: Who gets to write the next page
title.curious: Proof of work, and why it was chosen
title.technical: Proof of work, LWMA retarget, median time past

plain: Roughly once a minute, someone gets to add a page to the ledger. Who? Whoever first solves a puzzle that can only be solved by trying: no shortcut, no cleverness, just electricity and time.
That sounds wasteful, and it is the point. Rewriting old history would mean redoing all of that work, faster than everyone else is doing new work. That is what makes the past hard to change.
The winner is paid in new CAIRN. This is the only way CAIRN is ever created, which means the only way to get some at the start is to do the work, or to be paid by someone who did.
curious: Proof of work rather than proof of stake, and the reason is the start rather than the steady state. Proof of stake needs an initial distribution before it can work, which means founders deciding who holds power on day one. Proof of work needs nobody to decide anything: the network opens, and the first block goes to whoever mines it.
Difficulty adjusts every block over a 90 block window, with solve times clamped and a factor of four cap per retarget, so a large miner arriving or leaving does not strand the chain.
technical: LWMA over 90 blocks, clamped solve times, maximum 4x per retarget. Timestamps are validated against the median of the previous eleven blocks rather than against the parent, which removes the single-block manipulation that a later-than-parent rule permits.
Fork choice is by cumulative work, not length. Ties keep the branch already followed. Reorganisations are applied atomically, with undo records per active-chain block.

title.technical: The emission schedule and its rationale

plain: Nobody was given CAIRN at the start. There was no sale, no founder allocation, no reserve. On the day a network opens, the total in existence is zero, and every single unit since has come from paying for the work of finding a block.
The payment starts at 50 CAIRN per block and halves roughly every two years. It does not fall forever: it stops at a small figure, one hundredth of a CAIRN per block, and stays there.
Roughly 105 million CAIRN exist by the time it reaches that floor.
curious: 50 CAIRN initially, halving every 1051200 blocks, which is about two years at a one minute block time. The schedule bottoms out at a permanent tail of 0.01 CAIRN per block, giving around 105 million CAIRN before the tail dominates.
The smallest unit is the pebble: one hundred million pebbles make one CAIRN, the same granularity Bitcoin uses.
technical: The tail is a deliberate design choice, not an oversight. Whether transaction fees alone can fund security in the long run is an open question, and a chain whose central promise is verifiability in thirty years cannot rest its security budget on an open question.
The cost is a known, small, and permanently decreasing rate of dilution, which is a price worth paying for a security budget that does not depend on a fee market existing.

title.plain: What you still have to take on faith

plain: Two things worth saying out loud. First, Cairn is new and unproven. It has not been attacked, it has not been audited by outsiders, and the current network is a test network whose money is worth nothing and which will be wiped.

Second, joining for the first time still means downloading the whole history. Every block carries what is needed to make that unnecessary, and the part that uses it is not written yet. So today a newcomer downloads everything; the day that work is done, a newcomer downloads about a thousandth of it and checks it just as thoroughly.
It is written here rather than left for you to find.
curious: Initial sync still downloads and revalidates every block. Steady state cost is flat, first-start cost is not, and the fix is half done: every header now commits to the work behind the chain and to every header before it, so a newcomer can be given a sample rather than the lot. What is missing is the protocol that serves that sample.

Measured, at one block a minute: thirty years of a busy chain is about forty eight gigabytes to download and five hours to revalidate. Through the sample it is a few hundred kilobytes of headers plus the hundred megabytes of state, checked against the commitment in the tip. No checkpoint, no trusted snapshot, nobody to believe.

One cost also still grows: a node holds every block of the branch it follows in memory. That is the history, not the state it validates against, and the same commitment is what will let it stop. Smaller: an archivist rebuilds a proof in time proportional to the set it holds.
technical: No external audit yet, and none of the cryptography is novel: BLAKE3 with per-domain derived keys, Ed25519 with small-order and non-canonical encodings rejected at construction. Novelty is in the state layout, which is where it should be if anywhere.

Deadlines, connection ceilings, per address shares, temporary refusal, bounded undo records and bounded send queues are all in place, so nothing an anonymous peer does decides how much a node spends. Headers commit to cumulative work and to a forest of every earlier header, which is what a sampled start needs and what could not have been added after a network had value on it. What is left: the sampling protocol itself, moving the history out of memory, and a leaner hot tree representation.

plain: You can look at the rules the network runs on, watch blocks arriving live, or run a node yourself. Running one is the only way to check any of this without taking someone else at their word, and it is the point of the whole design.
curious: The consensus parameters are read live from the node. The explorer shows the chain as that node sees it. Running your own is a few minutes of work and removes this page from your trust assumptions entirely.
technical: Parameters live from ConsensusParams, chain state from the followed branch. The source is public and the dependency tree is deliberately small: blake3, ed25519-dalek, getrandom, thiserror, zeroize.

plain: A node is the program that checks the chain for you. Running one means you stop taking anyone at their word, including this website. It needs no special hardware and no permission from anybody.
curious: A full validating node, with a bounded state, on ordinary hardware. Download it below, or build it from source at the end of this page.
technical: Built in the open by GitHub from a tagged commit, with an attestation tying every file to the commit and the workflow that produced it. The check is made against GitHub, not against us.

warning.title: Read this first
body: This is a test network. The CAIRN on it is worth nothing, and it is meant to be worth nothing.
The network will be reset. When it is, every balance on it disappears and nothing is carried over to any future network. Do not buy it, do not sell it, do not accept it as payment.
Cairn has not been audited. Do not put anything you care about on it.

get.title: Download

plain: Three programs in one folder. There is nothing to install: you unpack it, you run it, and if you delete the folder afterwards nothing of it is left on your machine.
curious: A node, a wallet, and this website, each a single file with no runtime to install alongside it. The Linux builds are linked against musl, so they start on machines older than the one that built them.
technical: Five targets, built on GitHub runners from the toolchain this repository pins and the dependency versions in Cargo.lock, with build provenance attested. The archive name carries no version, so this link is permanent; the version is in the folder inside it, in a VERSION file, and in what each program prints when it starts.

get.unknown: Your machine was not recognised, so nothing is picked out for you. The whole list is below.
get.phone: These are programs for a computer. A wallet you can carry in your pocket is not built yet; when it is, it will be a node too.
get.inside: Inside: a node, a wallet, the explorer that serves this site, both licences, and a short text saying what to do with them.

check.title: Check what you downloaded

plain: A program is the one thing on this site you cannot read for yourself. Here is what to do instead of believing us: ask GitHub which commit produced this exact file. The answer comes from GitHub's own records, and there is nothing we could do to change it.
curious: The first command needs the GitHub command line tool and checks the build provenance attestation. The second prints the hash of the file, which you compare against the SHA256SUMS published beside it.
technical: Provenance is recorded in a public transparency log and names the repository, the commit and the workflow. A file that verifies came out of that workflow on a runner nobody here controls. It says nothing about whether the source is good, only that the binary came from the source you can read.

warning: Your operating system will warn you about these programs. macOS will say it cannot check them for malicious software, and Windows will say it blocked an unrecognised app. Both are saying the same true thing: nobody bought a certificate, so there is no name to show you.
On macOS, tell it where the files came from: xattr -d com.apple.quarantine cairnd cairn-wallet cairn-explorer

That warning deserves more attention than it usually gets. If you would rather not run somebody else's binary at all, the last section on this page builds the same three programs from source in one command.

plain: That is the whole thing. It already knows where to start, so it finds other computers by itself, downloads the chain, and checks every rule as it goes. It prints a line every ten seconds saying where it stands. Stop it with Ctrl-C; start it again and it picks up where it left off.
curious: The addresses it starts from are written into the program, exactly as the first block is. It resolves them, asks whoever answers for more addresses, and from then on keeps its own book and never needs that list again. Nothing about the rules can be set on the command line: they come from the network name only.
technical: Add --archive to keep the cold set and be able to rebuild proofs for other people, which costs a set that grows. Add --seed to start somewhere else, which replaces the written-in list rather than adding to it. --keep bounds the blocks held on disk, one gigabyte by default. An unknown option is a hard error rather than something quietly ignored.

plain: The first command makes a secret key on your own machine. The second shows the address people pay you at. The third opens the wallet as a page in your browser, served by your own computer. The secret never leaves it, and it is never sent to this website or to anybody else. If you lose that file the money is gone: nobody, including us, can give it back.
curious: The wallet is a node. It does not ask a server what it owns; it joins the network, verifies the chain itself, and reads its balance out of the ledger it validated. The page it opens is served on the loopback and nowhere else, behind a secret carried in the address.
technical: Ed25519. The key file is written with restrictive permissions and is never overwritten. The wallet keeps its own inclusion proofs for notes that have fallen to the cold set and refreshes them as the forest grows, so a cold spend needs no third party.

plain: This is how you get CAIRN on a test network. Your computer starts looking for blocks, and when it finds one the reward goes to your address. There is no other way to get any: nobody has a stock to hand out.
curious: Single-threaded mining inside the node, which is enough for a test network. Rewards go to the key you name, and that key can live anywhere: the node is told an address and never sees the secret behind it.
technical: The opening difficulty of testnet-6 is 2^27, calibrated so the first block takes roughly the target block time on one ordinary core, at a measured 2.29 million hashes per second.

plain: A network needs computers that stay on. If you rent a server, this puts a node on it as a service: it starts again by itself after a reboot, and it keeps running when you close the terminal.
curious: Debian or Ubuntu with systemd, which is what almost every rented server runs. It builds from source rather than downloading a binary, so what runs on your machine is what you can read, creates an unprivileged user with no shell, and opens the port if ufw is there.
technical: Read install.sh before running it; it is short and it says what it does. No wallet key ever goes on a machine like this. Mining does not break that rule: the node is given a public address and nothing else, and the key that spends the rewards stays wherever you keep it.

plain: This website is one of the three programs in the folder you downloaded. It serves these exact pages from your own machine, reading your own node. Nothing here needs to be taken on trust either.
curious: The explorer is a node that also builds an index and serves the site. The index is a cost that grows with the chain, which is precisely why it lives here and not in the node everybody runs.
technical: The site is compiled into the binary; nothing is read from disk at runtime. The HTTP layer is standard library only, one thread per connection, GET and HEAD, no request body.

Unlike a node, the explorer keeps every block on disk by default rather than a gigabyte of them. It builds its index by walking the chain from the first block up, so blocks dropped off the bottom are the ones it needs most. Use --keep to bound it anyway; the site then says on every page that it has only read the chain from the oldest block it still holds.

plain: You need Rust, which is a free programming toolchain. These three commands fetch the source and build it, and take a couple of minutes. What you end up with is the same three programs, built by you.
curious: Rust 1.89, which the repository pins so that everybody builds with the same one. Six direct dependencies and no asynchronous runtime.
technical: Rust 1.89. The workspace forbids unsafe code and denies arithmetic side effects, indexing, slicing, unwrap, expect and panic. The release profile keeps overflow checks on.

warn.outdated: This website is running a program that is too old for the chain it is watching. The rules from block {height} need version {required}, and this program knows only version {known}. It stopped following the chain there on purpose, so the height, the money and the blocks below are from before that moment and will not move again. Whoever runs this site has to install a newer version.
warn.stranded: The node behind this page was handed the ledger at block {anchor} and had to check its own way to block {settlesAt} before it could stand behind it. The blocks in between never arrived, and it holds nothing below block {anchor}, so there is no other way to reach them. Nothing on this page has been checked by this node. Whoever runs this site has to start it again from scratch.
warn.probation: The node behind this page has not yet checked the chain it is showing you. It was handed a ledger by another computer and has checked {checked} of the {owed} blocks it has to check before it can stand behind it. Until then, everything below is somebody else's account of the chain rather than this node's own reading. It carries on by itself; wait for this line to go.
warn.joining: The node behind this page is still being handed the chain by another computer. Nothing below is complete yet, and some of it is missing rather than wrong. It carries on by itself.
warn.outOfReach: The node behind this page has been offered {blocks} blocks it cannot reach, which means somebody is following a chain that parts from this one further back than this node can see. It cannot cross to that chain however much of it arrives. What is below may not be what most of the network agrees on.
warn.indexEmpty: This page has not read the chain yet. It is working through {blocks} blocks, and until it has finished, every address on this site will say it holds nothing, because nothing has been read rather than because nothing is there. Balances shown now are not balances.
warn.indexPartial: This site cannot see the whole chain. It has only read from block {from} upwards, because the computer behind it no longer keeps the blocks below that. Every balance and every total here is about that part of the chain and not about the chain: an address that was paid earlier and has spent nothing since will show as empty. Whoever runs this site can fix it by keeping every block.
warn.indexBehind: This site is {blocks} blocks behind the chain. What is below was true a while ago. Anything paid or spent since is not here yet.
warn.alone: The computer behind this page is not connected to anybody. It is showing you the chain as it last saw it, and it will not learn about a new block until somebody reaches it again.
warn.supply: The two ways this site counts the money in existence do not agree: the chain's own accounts say {issued} CAIRN and adding up the notes gives {counted} CAIRN. They are worked out from different things and should be the same number. One of them is wrong and this page cannot tell you which.

foot.watching: This page only reads. It holds no key, it can sign nothing, and it will never ask you for one.
